comments.text:
Shrinkflation is necessary unfortunately given our economic situation. If companies instead just raise prices it causes sticker shock that makes people go to competitor brands, so they are basically forced by consumer behavior to effectively scam you in order to turn a profit. For food and other grocery store items in particular that tend to have a fairly low profit margin the end result is effectively the same either way. The result: the prices have gone up significantly for goods in our society in recent years, without corresponding increases to wages that would allow the average person to afford the new prices.

If wages had kept pace with inflation over the last 10-15 years (or better yet were even remotely close to the overall growth in the economy), this would be a non-issue.

Don't forget what the core issue is. People feel scammed because they have to pay more for less, but that's not ultimately due to shrinkflation itself.

comments.text:
I think this video spends a little bit too much time and emphasis on "corporate greed" and how corporations are increasing prices significantly more than inflation.

"Shrinkflation" is a deceptive practice and should be at a minimum shunned if not outright banned. However, straight price increases is just free market economy: Supply and demand. There's nothing "unethical" about a company asking whatever they want for their product. If they want to ask a million dollars for a candy bar, that's their business. They can ask whatever they want.

The thing that keeps prices reasonable in a free market economy is competition: If one company asks a million dollars for a candy bar, and another one is selling an extremely similar candy bar for 50 cents, guess which one the customers will buy. That's how it works. That's how it should work.

Shrinkflation = genuinely bad and unethical. Increasing prices = normal economy; companies are free to set the prices how they want, competitors will keep them in check.

I have a grocery checklist on my iPhone (notes app). 
I check my fridge and pantry and untick items I need to buy on my weekly Saturday morning shopping.
I also have the Coles app with a list of my commonly bought items.
I check to see which items are on sale then untick them on my iPhone list even if I have enough to last week or two.
I buy those items in bulk, usually to last through the 2 or 4 week “price reduction” cycle. 
I tick off the items I buy from my iPhone list as I shop. This helps keep my average shopping costs down while minimising my chance of wandering around the isles buying things I don’t need or already have a good stock at home. 
Try it. 
Make and use those lists. 
You’ll see the savings results very fast!

They opened a specialty dunkin in a high end mall charging 20 to 30 pesos for extra large donuts even bigger than the old ones but again not optimized so texture and flavor were off. This didnt last long as rich people didnt take to dunkin which is normally a childs treat here. Dunkin was also competing with gonuts donuts, a fancy local donut place trying to copy krispy kremes glazed donuts which rich kids were bringing home by the box after traveling. Dunkin had no answer and seemed content to suck.

Eventually krispy kreme opened stores here, selling donuts at 40 pesos, quite a luxury a decade ago, but popular enough that it killed hot loops which spent its last pathetic years making super weird new flavors and constantly offering discounts and promos before going to donut heaven. 

Krispy kreme is still cool enough for lower middle to middle class people but the new niche fancy place is jco which is content to be fairly exclusive with its weird ass flavors reminiscent of california pizza kitchens  abominable frankenstein anti pizzas. 

Meanwhile dunkin returned to normal size for 20 pesos in the late 2010s and has finally risen to 25 to 40 pesos for the classic staple donuts and almost any higher amount for their seasonal donuts.

comments.text:
The thing this video misses badly is the cost of doing business. The term "profits" in financial reports generally refer to gross profits, which are the profits a company makes before tax, wages, buying product, rent, etc.. If any of those increase cost inflation happens as gross profits need increase to maintain the current trajectory. The core issue is that the government in the west try their hardest to avoid have the consumer/voter feel the issue of their political choices made during covid by increasing social spending, minimum wage increases and other such political actions (on top of the increasing elderly population, increasing low skilled migration and other such things that already happening). This increased cost of doing business which increased pricing, which governments reacted to by doing the same thing again, which increased the cost of doing business, etc., etc. 

So yea, sure not all price increases and shrinking products (that just product cost inflation, note that that's different from currency inflation). And business rather reduce quality of reduce volume, especially in the food sector because consumers HATE price increases even minor ones. But the core issue is increased cost of doing business by politicians to avoid the negative effects of the choices they made and than blame any and all business' as a whole. And of course some business will abuse the current market situation, but they only can do that because of the current market situation. If it's all business just being greedy for the sake of being greedy, like some people assume, it would be very easy for a new company to compete.

The only hard solution is simply to significantly reduce the cost of doing business by reducing taxation (and by extension government spending) and decrease non-tax costs of doing business (like minimum wage laws), which will normalize prices. Yes, that sucks but political actions have consequences.

comments.text:
This is an exercise in confusion by conflating different subjects, so that there is always someone else to blame, some alternative narrative to escape responsibility. Let's separate them, to not be manipulated.

 - Inlfation was caused in this case by the politics of credit expansion and other equivalents of money printing. "Stimulus" programs and other debt games have increased the amount of money moving around.
 - Misleading customers is fraud. Whether the fraudulent narrative concerns inflation is incidental. Why most fraud is legal in most nations is an interesting question, but this is not specific to shrinkflation.
 - Rising profits in a competitive market cannot be a permanent phenomenon, as any competitor counteracting the change gains market share. This is an attempt to find a scapegoat, not analysis of causes.
 - Greed is a similarly strange thing to blame for a sudden change, given that greedy people have existed since time immemorial. It is a bit like blaming gravity for a car accident. Maybe not false, but misleading.

All that said, I suspect this analysis of being overly careful and humble, to the point of becoming dull, to avoid stepping on any ego.

If you needlessly kept buying from companies who are clearly trying to exploit you, voted in favor of magic "help" by centralized credit expansion, or supported lax justice and leaving the overhead of countering "lesser" crimes such as fraud to victims, you are at fault for the respective outcome.

Most likely, a majority in this comment section is guilty of these causes. Which doesn't feel good to the ego, so it's gotta be the fault of that other party, greedy corporations, or whatever. And this is the real cause. It is the Vision of the Anointed. Addressing that would mean recognizing that the line between good and evil cuts through the heart of every man (and woman and girl and so on)... not always only the others'.

comments.text: One of the ways to combat this would be labeling legislation requiring retailers to advertise the unit rate as the primary price. Retailers will often advertise the product price and then provide a unit rate (eg $/litre) in fine print, flip this and require the unit rate to be the prominent price. Markets only work when buyers can make informed decisions. Any effort to improve the buyer’s access to information puts downward pressure on supplier’s sneaky tactics. Perhaps the real reason for all of this can be of two essential reasons.
1: The the stock market share price
2: Monopolisation of the market

Most corporations these days have  their valuations based upon a share price. That share price determines how much money corporations and their owners can borrow to finance their activities and future expansion or maintain current viability of running the business all courtesy of banks seeing a profit to lend money based upon such speculation, not real world economics . That share price is  determined upon expectations and desire of the market for future "growth", and that growth comes from expectations of growing into becoming a future monopoly and what wealth that corporation can extract from being that monopoly through its profits, even if those profits can never pay off the debts incurred. So long as the share price is growing at 10+%, that corporation maintains its dominance and existence, and the one way to do that is through  its profit margins that need to expand every year to serve its debt and satisfy shareholder expectations. And hey presto, to expand profits in a market that has reached its zenith and in the real world can not grow any more or expand to new gain customers or consumers, you increase prices to existing customers and do so by trying such practices like shrinkflation.

The second reason is that once a monopoly has been achieved, or have a small enough conglomerate of cartel corporations, prices increase because of the reasoning of having a captured market or dependence upon the corporation or cartel, where else can one go to get a product or service. So a corporation can increase prices until a critical price of what the market can bare is found.  Right now that search is being conducted by corporations who are looking for that level of what the market can bare, and corporate  greedflation is at hand to take advantage of this while it lasts because there is little to no counter to it as alternatives do not exist.

comments.text:
Here's the thing.... People's buying habits when it comes to regular purchases like groceries really doesn't change all that much, we all know more or less what we want to buy in a week and have a core-set of things we purchase every week Bread, milk,egg, cereal, some type of protein, rice or spaghetti that make up a large portion of our purchases at a grocery store. 

Aside from some brief spikes there was almost no change to demand for the majority of consumer goods (aside from electronics), some demand actually went down for things like Oil and Gas during the pandemic, there were times where production fell behind and factories closed such as major  meat packing facilities and automakers but broadly speaking demand remained unchanged. The problem appeared when so-called well educated economists started saying there was too much spending during COVID and we were at risk of run away inflation,  not understanding that unlike almost any other time in history the average person was provided money that went directly back into the economy and it was taking place globally. 

Historically if there is  run-away inflation its the results of a major war (such as WW)  where Germany was saddled with the majority of the debt/damages or some huge economic collapse taking place in a single country resulting in mass unemployment. They were localized issues and involved the Government spending huge amounts of money to try and keep up with interest payments and purchase goods from other countries with a comparatively worthless currency. 

But because economists were so sure  there would be mass inflation exiting  COVID it actually became a self fulfilling prophecy and that "Little bit more" mentioned in the video. The problem is that customers have to take this on the chin because unlike so many other industries where we will simply go somewhere else or stop buying a product we are entirely at the mercy of grocery stores when it comes to food if a few of them take the opportunity to raise prices. It can take years to get a functional garden working with a few live stock animals provided you even have the space for it and  there isn't enough animals in and around cities for hunting to sustain them for long. 

We are stuck in a situation where we need large scale farming and livestock facilities to produce huge amounts of food to feed everyone and that is an issue that will take decades to fix, there isn't going to be a good way for a smaller company to come in an undercut existing companies with better or cheaper products at any type of reasonable scale to meet demand and if they do they are swiftly bought out by larger companies. 

So there really is no defending corporations who took the opportunity to jack up prices during the pandemic and we should have gone after them with criminal charges and heavy fines.... But at a near global level nothing.

comments.text:
Key ideas
The video starts with examples of everyday products getting smaller (burgers, cereal boxes, paper towels, muffin packs) while prices stay the same or rise, illustrating “shrinkflation” as a hidden price increase.​

It explains that classic inflation was initially driven by factors like supply chain disruptions, higher raw material costs, wages, and global shocks, which raised input costs for firms.​​

Shrinkflation is described as one way companies protected or boosted profits when traditional grocery and consumer-goods businesses already operated on thin margins.​​

Greedflation and skimpflation
The video then shows that in many sectors, prices kept rising even after input costs (like energy and commodities) started falling, which is where the term “greedflation” comes in: companies using the inflation narrative to pad profit margins.​​

It notes that this pattern has been observed in places like Canada, the UK, Australia, the EU, and the US, where corporate profits rose faster than costs for some product lines.​​

“Skimpflation” is introduced as another tactic, where firms quietly downgrade ingredients, materials, or service quality while keeping prices the same, so consumers pay the same for a worse product.​​

Overall message
The core argument is that today’s higher prices are not purely about macroeconomic inflation; a non-trivial share in some categories is explained by companies shrinking sizes, cutting quality, and using market power to maintain or expand profits.​​

The video emphasizes that this leaves consumers feeling like they are “paying more for less” and that understanding these mechanisms—shrinkflation, greedflation, and skimpflation—is key to recognizing when price hikes are driven by necessity versus opportunism.​​

Amazing video like always.

However, I believe it's important to know the type of costs. At the most basic levels, almost all costs can be split into fixed and variables costs.
When, for example, sizes are reduced, the fixed costs usually stay the same, however variables costs might go down.
When talking about increases of input prices in %, is this the full cost or just variables costs? If so, has the company adjusted their expenses in any way that might increase fixed costs and decrease variables costs? Do these changes affect the future of how they can change prices? How would this show in gross margins, could that show a false result of such reports?
It is clear that greed and inflation are both causes, however overall if people end up paying it means they still believe it to be worth it.

For me, the most noticeable shrinkflation has been with Halloween candy for kids.  I remember when "fun sized" bars were bigger.  They used to be roughly 1/3 of a full sized bar, and "fun sized" Reese's cups were 1 full sized cup (instead of the 2 in a standard package).  Now, "fun sized" is substantially smaller, closer to the size of a Hershey's Kiss than a candy bar.  As a result, I switched to handing out full sized candy bars for Halloween (Note - I live in an area where I get very few trick or treaters, which is why I can afford to do this).
[Edit - added additional thoughts] I suspect regulations, if governments are willing to listen to the people rather than the big $ they rely on for election funds, would be the biggest help.  The problem is more complex than just corporate greed, so this proposition is probably overly simplistic.  I think we need regulations to force both fair wages and disclosure/fair pricing.  This will, of course, cause problems.  Due to the nature of the stock market, corporations feel immense pressure to maintain the illusion of continuing growth.  It's not enough just to be profitable; they have to keep growing in order to keep their investors happy.  Blocking off their ability to squeeze consumers as much will just force them to get more creative and find other ways to maintain that illusion.

comments.text:
Blaming it on "greed" is like blaming plane crashes on gravity.  It's a way to skip thinking - it doesn't tell you anything about the 'cause and effect'.  It takes millions of buyers and sellers, each trying to maximize the value they get from an exchange, to arrive at prices for scarce resources.  When Lays makes their 10 'potato chips covered in vegetable oil and salt', they don't actually know who they're competing with for the vegetable oil, the components that make it, or the resources it takes to manufacture and move those components.  They might be competing with people who manufacture toy frisbees or distribute other chemicals in the same drums or tankers.  They're probably competing with tens of thousands of seemingly unrelated products on a global level.  It's folly to pretend it can be planned, because you think they're "greedy".  

Economic laws are laws.  Increasing the amount of dollars chasing the same amount of goods will make your dollars buy less.  Fixing prices with ceilings and floors will invariably lead to shortages.  During the Cold War, the Soviets were copying prices out of Sears catalogues because they couldn't generate that critical information on their own, without markets. 

And for God's sake, please think long and hard about the cavalcade of morons we have on Capital Hill, and how competently less than a thousand people ( including Maxine Waters and Margery Taylor Green - pick your bad guys ) can craft economic policy for the other 330 million Americans that have to live under it.  If you think they can manage healthcare distribution and global trade, you're handing the next "George Santos / Michele Bachmann" the keys to the bus.

comments.text: Working for a producer of fmcg goods in europe. You are correctwith your conclusions but a bit off as to the mechanics of how this happens. Imagine a supply chain of just three parties before the consumer. Producer, distributor and retailer. Say input for a chocolate bar costs 1€ and the cost increases by 10% and now costs 1,1€. On the shelf of the retailer it used to cost 3€. It would be logical to assume that the new price would be 3,1€. However, every party in the chain increses by 10% to maintain margin. So if the producer increses by 10%, distributor increses by 10%, and retailer increses by 10%. Net effect is that the end price would be closer to 4€ than 3,1€. We use shrinkflation because in that way we do not compound price increase that ends up higher than increase in input but only the increase in input costs are transferred to the consumer.

comments.text: “Thin margins” as a term is subjective and deceptive. “Thin” itself is the pivot word - the adjective. Thin to the corporate shareholders could be when profits drop below what most of us would consider an acceptable threshold. Instead of making 20% profit over expenses, it now makes 10% which causes panic among investors even though they are still in the black. After salaries and expenses, the pile of money grows less quickly even though the money itself sits stagnant with no apparent purpose other than a catastrophic rainy day emergency. So, the greedy investors decide to either short the product or service or raise prices to maintain a perception of acceptability. The investors fudge this or that to keep up the charade - a vanity contest. They maintain while those downstream must sacrifice. This is a recipe for disaster if left unchecked. So, the bank steps in to do just that by raising interest rates. This shifts profit from businesses investors to the bank investors. This encourages producers of goods and services to stop producing and begin lending money at interest. Now, we have less production and more competition among lenders. Price wars level up while they race to the bottom.

comments.text: Germany used to have fixed sizes for certain products. For chocolate bars for instance, the allowed values were 75, 100, 125, 150, 200, 250, 300, 400, and 500 grams per bar. Any consumer could easily spot the difference between them, so manufacturers had a much harder time hiding price hikes by shrinking the package. Unfortunately, the EU made us get rid of that law. Now it's common place that a formerly 100 gram bar suddenly has 95, 90 or 85 grams (obviously without advertising the change). The worst offender is Milka, which has bars in all sorts of sizes - they're all in the same display, all have the same physical footprint, but they're all different. It's simply a scam.

comments.text:
I work at an FMCG company. What I can say is that, for a lot of companies that aren't industry leaders and have an embedded sets of customers as well as have limited margins? It's a painful necessity. Otherwise? Likely IS mainly greed.

Something a lot of people don't realize is that changing your SKUs costs - from development, to changing process, distribution, compensation to distributors and sellers, likely requiring discounts to compete... This doesn't even get to the product competitiveness once it gets to the market.

But! I've seen those Profit and Loss analysis. In the long term, it can indeed save a lot of money. I can buy a company that isn't gigantic HAS to do all these to be able to absorb further shocks and tougher market sentiments and purchasing powers. Especially if they want to retain employees - whether due to genuine sense of responsibility by the leaders or the pragmatism of talent retention.

If they don't care about all that, and they're either leads the industry in terms of marketshare and mindshare, especially if they're targeting higher class market, then a lot of it likely is greed. If you see enough people doing shrinkflation, you might as well do do because you'd just be leaving money on the table otherwise.

"Free market" competition only works when anyone with a dream and a passion can start up a company and compete on equal terms. Anything bigger than that should, must be syndicalised and owned by the people who do the work, or socialised and owned by the community at large.
